patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Kim is a 73-year-old right-handed Korean-American retired accountant who is referred to neurology by his orthopedic surgeon for persistent left shoulder stiffness and left arm movement difficulty that has not responded adequately to treatment for adhesive capsulitis over the past 18 months. He is accompanied by his adult son, who provides additional history.

Approximately two years ago, the patient and his family noticed that he no longer swung his left arm when walking. He and his wife attributed this initially to getting older. About 18 months ago he began experiencing left shoulder aching and stiffness with restricted range of motion. He was evaluated by orthopedic surgery, who diagnosed left-shoulder adhesive capsulitis based on restricted passive and active range of motion. Plain films showed no fracture; ultrasound showed no rotator cuff tear. He received two corticosteroid injections into the left glenohumeral joint and completed 12 weeks of physical therapy. His shoulder range of motion improved only marginally. A cervical spine MRI ordered at that time demonstrated C5-C6 spondylosis with mild foraminal narrowing, which the spine team considered unlikely to account for the shoulder-predominant picture. The orthopedic surgeon noted on his most recent visit that the shoulder stiffness had a different quality than typical frozen shoulder — the arm just did not move naturally — and has now referred him to neurology.

On direct neurological questioning today, the patient and his son report that over the past 12 to 15 months the patient's left hand has developed an intermittent trembling at rest, which stops when he reaches for something and returns when his hand is in his lap. He has noticed increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks on the left: buttoning shirts is labored, and his handwriting has become smaller. His son notes that his father appears to move more slowly in general, takes longer to rise from chairs, and shuffles more than before. The patient reports diminished sense of smell over the past two years, which he had not previously mentioned to any physician. He also reports worsening constipation and occasional lightheadedness when standing quickly. His wife has told him that he sometimes acts out his dreams at night — she has been kicked twice. He denies hallucinations, significant cognitive decline beyond mild word-finding difficulty, and denies any falls to date.

He takes no medications known to cause parkinsonism. He has never taken antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine.
